wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.name: White Salmon Lodge road
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.notes: Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder. Going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.
hazards: avalanche off the Hanging Glacier across the approach basin
brush in the valley bottom without snow cover
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
Winnie's Slide holds firm ice when it has melted back
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.baseFinding:
The route proper begins at the foot of the White Salmon Glacier, or from the bivy sites up and right of it. Ascend the glacier weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses; the marker you are climbing toward is the base of Winnie's Slide at roughly 6,800 ft. Winnie's Slide is unmistakable once you are under it — the angle jumps to around forty to forty-five degrees for roughly a rope length, and it is the only thing on this side of the mountain that steepens like that. Above it you step onto the Upper Curtis Glacier.

If you are still on low-angle glacier threading around rock islands, you are below the slide, however long you have been walking. Conversely, if you have topped out on flatter glacier without a steep pitch behind you, you have drifted off the line and are somewhere else on the White Salmon.

wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.
hazards: a committing descent at the start that must be reclimbed on the way out
Hanging Glacier avalanche debris across the valley
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.baseFinding: Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft is still the reference feature low on the route; higher, the head of the White Salmon is marked by the base of Hell's Highway. Neither is a subtle feature — both are abrupt steepenings out of low-angle glacier.

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: This is the standard approach to Mount Skokomish. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101 and about 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake trailhead, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.baseFinding:
Stand at Lake of the Angels and the cirque itself tells you which way to go: Mount Stone is on your right, another peak is on your left, and Mount Skokomish is straight ahead. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

The turn is around the right-hand side of the lake, on a way trail heading west to the ridge. Then take a broad gully southwest and up toward the saddle just north of point 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud.

Second test, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours south and southwest across scree, grass and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn. The tarn is the confirmation. Turn right and start climbing when you are above the large tarn — that is the trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

Third test, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around left to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has three summit horns and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

A directional warning: contouring too far right (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut west over the ridge instead.

wa_mount_skokomish_standard.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.notes: This is not the standard approach, but it is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford Huckleberry Creek at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot root and rock ladders, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail. Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — near the area burned by the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire
wa_mount_skokomish_standard.baseFinding: The base on this side is the open basin and saddle beneath the south peak at about 5,500 ft, and the test for it is underfoot: the footing turns to loose, rotten rock from there up. Below the saddle you are fighting brush and heather; at and above it you are on scree and shattered rock. That transition is the arrival cue and it does not require seeing anything. The test for the approach itself is the root ladder, because it is the one unmistakable feature on this trail: about a thousand feet of hand-and-foot climbing on roots and rock in roughly half a mile, one pitch near vertical, topping out on a ridge at about 4,100 ft. If you have not used your hands, you are not on the Mildred Lakes trail. And the trail then descends off that ridge to the lakes — a trail that keeps climbing past 4,100 ft is not this one. The limit of this approach: the ground between the Mildred Lakes and Skokomish's south peak is unmaintained, brushy and easy to lose, with no marker sequence published for it. The standard route is on the Putvin side. Take this approach only if you have a reason to be at the Mildred Lakes, and expect to navigate rather than to follow.

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.
hazards: Boat access from Ross Lake Resort must be booked; no road out if plans slip
Slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin at 2,900 ft
Loose moraine between the lake and the glacier toe
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Silver Glacier; the glacier is thinning so lines shift yearly
Class 4 summit-block step on loose, lichen-covered rock
Long, committing retreat from a high camp
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.baseFinding:
From the Silver Lake camp the route does not go near a col. Walk round the north side of the lake to its far, south-west end, then head south across moraine and snow, skirting a small rock buttress, to the toe of the glacier at about 7,400 ft. Allow an hour to an hour and a half from camp.

You should be able to see at least the lower glacier from camp, so pick your line onto it before you leave. The ice comes down toward the lake from the north side of the peak; you rope up at its toe and climb it, with no saddle or gully on the way.

The wide gully and the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west belong to the other approach, from the lake on the Depot Creek side. If you are climbing a gully toward a gap, you have left this line.

And the negative marker that matters most: the south-west route on this peak starts at the toe of a different glacier on the other flank, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
hazards: International border crossing on foot; passports needed
Wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line at Depot Creek Falls, the crux of the walk-in
Overgrown approach road that washes out and lengthens the walk
Crevasses and a bergschrund on the Silver Glacier beyond the Custer-Spickard saddle
Class 4 summit-block step on loose, lichen-covered rock
Taking the wrong route from the shared Ouzel Lake camp costs a day
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.baseFinding:
From the Depot Creek camp, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully that leads to the col.

The fixed point is the same: the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully you came up is the way back to camp; the glacier lies on the far side.

The test that you are at the right gap is that both summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

Do not confuse this start with the south-west route, which leaves the same camp. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. If you have not gained a col, you are not on this route.

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
hazards: Border crossing on foot; passport needed, with a register at the obelisk
Washed-out road lengthens the walk without warning
Wet slick boulders and slabs at Depot Creek Falls with an old fixed hand-line of unknown condition
Crevasses on the southwest glacier, including a marginal snow bridge on the standard line
Short steep loose rock gully at the glacier head, then loose Class 2-3 ribs and gullies near the summit
30-40 degree snow near the summit ridge
Extreme remoteness, no cell coverage
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.baseFinding:
The critical instruction is that you leave the drainage before the pass, not at it. From camp, ascend the broad talus couloir and stream drainage north to north-east toward the saddle at roughly 7,200 ft - but well before reaching that saddle, cut right around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather and moraine basins.

The negative marker is exact and easy to use: if you have arrived at the saddle and are looking down into the cirque on the far side, you have gone too far. Go back down and find the buttress toe.

The buttress toe is the feature - a steep rock nose that the couloir runs past on its left. Turning its foot puts you into open heather and moraine, which is different ground from the couloir you have been climbing, and that change underfoot is the confirmation.

The base is the toe of the south-west glacier, reached by traversing those basins. Rope up and put crampons on there rather than part-way across. The line up the ice is its climber's-right margin, which holds hard snow and ice at thirty to forty degrees and relatively few crevasses; about half-way up, one poor-looking crevasse has to be crossed on a marginal bridge, so probe it and expect it to be worse late in the season.

Confirm at the top of the ice: a short steep loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on a low col on the south-west ridge, above the cirque. That col is where the summit scramble starts. If the ice runs you out onto a broad snow shoulder with no gully and no col, you have taken the glacier's centre or its left side instead of its right margin.

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
hazards: Boat access must be booked; no road out
Slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin at 2,900 ft
Long carry to a high camp at about 6,763 ft
Crevasses on the glaciers either side of the divide, including a marginal snow bridge on the southwest glacier
Short steep loose rock gully at the glacier head and loose Class 2-3 rock near the summit
Camp is on the opposite side from Depot Creek, so col-based descriptions can mislead
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.baseFinding:
The old cabin at about 2,900 ft is the proof you are on the right side of the creek. The trail climbs the north side; if you have not passed a cabin by the time the trail gives out, you are on the wrong bank and should cross before the cross-country starts, not after.

Above the cabin the markers are occasional blazes on trees rather than tread. Blazes that stop appearing mean you have drifted; the slide alder will let you keep going anyway, which is why this is worth checking rather than assuming.

The camp is the lake basin at about 6,763 ft, and from it the route to this peak's south-west side goes up and over toward the col between it and its neighbour to the north-west.

Be clear which route you are on when you arrive. From this side the natural line gains the col at about 7,380 ft between the two peaks, which is where the glacier route on the north side starts. The south-west route instead wants the toe of the south-west glacier, which is reached by traversing into open heather and moraine basins round the toe of a rock buttress, not by gaining a col. If you find yourself standing in a saddle between two summits, you are on the other route's start.

wa_mount_steel_standard.name: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
camps: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
wa_mount_steel_standard.notes: Twenty-odd miles up the Duckabush over Big Hump, with a wide ford of the river above Duckabush Camp that runs thigh-deep and swift in early season. The climbers' line leaves the maintained trail roughly three miles below Marmot Lake. A multi-day backpack with a high camp at the lake or in the basin, never a car-to-car day.
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Unmarked turnoff and unmapped off-trail travel above the amphitheater, easy to lose in fog
Wide Duckabush River ford above Duckabush Camp, thigh-deep and swift early season or after rain
Fallen timber and standing dead snags in the burned sections of the lower valley
Steep loose switchbacks on Big Hump, hard on tired legs
Extremely remote, rescue likely takes a day or more
wa_mount_steel_standard.baseFinding: The turnoff is unmarked — no sign, cairns at best — and getting it right is the whole navigation problem on this route. Above Duckabush Camp, watch for a small feeder creek coming in from climber's-left and follow it up out of the valley. It leads into a rocky amphitheater on the west side of the summit, and that amphitheater is the base: once you are standing in it the climbing is easy Class 2 heather and talus straight up to the summit ridge, so the hard part is behind you. The maintained trail runs on past the turnoff toward the pass, so if you find yourself gaining the pass or arriving at Marmot Lake you have walked past the creek and should drop back down the trail. Snow fills the amphitheater and the slopes above into summer and cornices build on the summit ridge into late June, so carry an axe and treat the crest as possibly unsupported. Water is dependable at the creek and scarce once you leave it — fill up before you start climbing.

wa_mount_steel_standard.name: First Divide and the unnamed lake basin

approachLogistics.trailhead: Staircase Trailhead (North Fork Skokomish, Olympic NP)

wa_mount_steel_standard.notes: Parties generally find this the easier of the two lines and it is much shorter, but the corridor on that side has been closed by fire damage — confirm before planning around it. From the divide the route runs west into a basin, then over a col and north along the crest.
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June; stay back from the eastern lip
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall on the closed valley corridor
Open basin ground that is easy to lose in fog
Loose talus on slopes either side of the col
Approach corridor closed since the fire, so access is not currently available
Turning the wrong way off the saddle commits you to a different peak
wa_mount_steel_standard.baseFinding: From First Divide, follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake. That lake is the marker for this whole variant — it is the only standing water in the basin and it sits directly below the two summit humps of Steel, so if you are in an open basin with no lake in it you are in the wrong one. From the lake, drop southwest to the saddle between those humps; the saddle is the base of the climb, and from it you turn north along the summit ridge for the final easy Class 2 stretch to the high point. The direction of that turn is the thing to get right. Duckabush lies beyond the same col to the southwest and reads as the higher, more striking mountain from below, so a party that turns the wrong way off the saddle ends up committed to a different peak. The early-summer cornice and unconsolidated-snow caution applies just as strongly on this side: the crest holds snow late and it is not always attached to the rock beneath it, so stay back from the eastern lip.

wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
camps: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
hazards: Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, slick when wet and worse descending
Rock headwall mid-trail needing hand-over-hand moves, sometimes a fixed handline
Little to no reliable water on the lower trail
Snow lingering on shaded steps and in the basin above the lake into summer
Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels; fog common and parties lose the route
Loose rock on the summit block with rockfall onto parties below
Ambiguous Class 3/4 crux and exposed unprotected summit block
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.baseFinding: The base of the climb is a notch in Mount Stone's west ridge, and the test for it is a turn you make before a gate. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward St. Peter's Gate — the obvious notch above the basin. Just before the gate, turn sharply left and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through. That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill. Second test, at the notch: turn right and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short low class 3 chimney to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line. Third test, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it. What the route's own timing says: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate. Fog warning specific to this mountain: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.

wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a contingency and staging site rather than the normal plan for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lena Lake Trailhead (Hamma Hamma Road, FR-25)

wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
hazards: Long off-trail route over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes near St. Peter's Gate
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
Fog on the upper mountain; parties have lost the route
Very long approach with limited bail options
Loose rock on the summit block and an ambiguous Class 3/4 crux
Exposed unprotected summit block
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.baseFinding: Coming from the east you arrive at St. Peter's Gate itself, which is the high point of the traverse at about 5,950 ft and an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side. From the gate there are two ways onto the peak and they are different climbs. The one this route describes is the west-ridge notch: go through the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the west ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse route's line, not this one. So the fog test for this variant is which side of the gate you end up on: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder. Above the notch the tests are identical to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 chimney to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a groove on the left that bends right to the true south summit.

wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble
wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir.notes: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin road-end parking at about 4,243 ft. A quarter mile of old mining road leads to a fork; take the right branch for Longs Pass. The trail climbs an open, south-facing hillside with essentially no shade — in July and August this is a pre-dawn start, not a preference. Longs Pass sits around 6,200-6,250 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the car in about two miles, and it is the single most useful place on the whole approach. From the pass, drop the steep loose scree on the north side, losing 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft. Cross the creek — there is a summer log crossing, and in high melt it is worth walking to find it rather than wading — then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail upvalley (west) a short way to the meadow and camps below the couloir's outlet. Good camps sit on the valley floor more or less straight south of where the couloir comes down, with a few more near the footlog. From camp a climbers' path threads the meadow to the toe of the couloir. This is also the standard descent for the North Ridge, West Ridge and most of the rest of Stuart, so expect to share it.
wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir.season: Jul-Sep, once the couloir has melted to talus
hazards: Sun-exposed hillside to Longs Pass with no water and no shade
Ingalls Creek can run high in early-season melt; find the summer log rather than fording blind
The couloir is loose top to bottom — sand, scree and unstable blocks; serious rockfall risk from parties above
Upper couloir braids into a maze of use-paths and cairns; genuinely confusing in cloud or at dawn/dusk
The 8,800 ft snowfield must be passed on the climber's left
wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir.baseFinding:
Look at the mountain from Longs Pass and settle the line there. It is the only point on the approach where the entire south face is laid out in front of you, and once you have dropped to the valley floor at 4,800 ft the couloir's mouth is one of several timbered gully mouths that all look alike from below and from inside the trees.

What you are aiming for: the couloir bottoms out in the meadow at roughly 4,800 ft, upvalley (west) of where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, and a beaten climbers' path leaves the meadow directly into it. It is a wide, sandy, scree-floored trough rather than a narrow cleft, and it runs unbroken for about 4,000 ft.

The confirmation that you are in the right gully comes about two thirds of the way up: a permanent snowfield around 8,800 ft, just south of the false summit. The established talus path passes it on the climber's left. Parties who take the right-hand side of that snowfield end up on much harder ground and have found old rappel-station remnants there — that is the tell that you have gone wrong, not a sign you are on route.

The couloir does not top out on the summit. It delivers you to the false summit at about 9,200 ft; the true summit at 9,415 ft is a class 2-3 scramble east along the ridge from there, and this is the second place parties in cloud go wrong — stopping at the false summit, or dropping off it in the wrong direction on the way down.

wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb
wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir.notes:
The same line, in a completely different medium. With the couloir snow-filled it is a straightforward steep snow climb rather than a scree grind, and many parties prefer it this way — but it demands axe and crampons, an early start, and a hard turnaround, because the whole thing faces south and softens fast.

FR 9737 is a gravel road that is not maintained through winter and is generally not clear until late June in a heavy year, so a genuinely early-season attempt means adding road miles on foot or ski. Check the road before committing.

The Longs Pass hillside carries avalanche exposure in winter and spring conditions, and the north-side drop to Ingalls Creek holds snow that can be firm and icy at dawn and slushy by mid-morning.
wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir.season: May-Jun as a snow route; road access is the limiting factor earlier
hazards: FR 9737 unmaintained in winter/spring — verify access before driving out
Avalanche exposure on the Longs Pass hillside and in the couloir itself
South-facing: wet-slide and rockfall risk build through the day, so an early turnaround is not optional
Firm/icy snow at dawn on the north side of Longs Pass
Uncontrolled glissade on descent
wa_mount_stuart_cascadian_couloir.baseFinding:
With snow cover the couloir reads far more clearly from the valley than it does in summer — it is the continuous white ribbon running the full height of the south face, and the timbered gully mouths that confuse people in August are buried. Still take the look from Longs Pass, because the valley-floor approach is in trees.

The 8,800 ft snowfield that is a landmark in summer is not a distinct feature when everything is snow, so the useful marker on the way up is the false summit at about 9,200 ft where the couloir ends. Do not treat topping out as summiting; the true summit is a scramble further east along the ridge.

On the descent in these conditions the risk inverts: the couloir is a glissade or boot-ski for most of its length and parties overrun themselves. Keep the axe in hand.

wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Mountaineer Creek valley to the 5,400 ft basin
wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier.notes: Start at the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, about 3,400 ft. Follow the main trail to the first fork, roughly two and a half to three miles in near 4,600 ft, and stay right for Stuart Lake. Left is Colchuck Lake, a different basin on the other side of the ridge. About a mile to a mile and a half past that junction, the Stuart Lake trail turns uphill and swings right, away from the water, and begins switchbacking. That turn is your cue. Leave the trail there and stay flat in the valley bottom with Mountaineer Creek. The test is simple and works in poor visibility: if you are gaining elevation on switchbacks you are walking to Stuart Lake and you have missed it. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs. There is no single canonical log and parties describe several sporty crossings that shift with the snowpack; early season, snowbanks make dropping onto a log awkward. On the far side, pick up the climbers' path along the creek. It is unmaintained, full of blowdown and re-routes, and the cairns are not to be trusted: they invite you up and right into a boulder slope around 4,675 ft. Two parties independently say stay low beside the creek instead, with the creek on your left — the path is unpleasant but the better line. Some parties do use the boulder field deliberately to avoid the creek crossings, so treat it as a genuine choice rather than a mistake. After about a mile and a half the valley steepens. Turn right and west and climb talus and forest into a hanging flat basin at about 5,400 ft, under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers. That right-turn-and-climb out of a steepening valley into flat ground is the arrival cue for the bivy.
wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier.season: Roughly Apr-Jun; the ice cliff and the couloir exit get harder and more broken as the season runs on
hazards: Serac fall from the hanging ice cliff you traverse beneath — a party watched a large piece break away and shatter on the ledge below them
Rockfall and avalanche in the couloir
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the lower glacier
A cornice at the couloir exit, which becomes the crux when large
An unmaintained climbers' trail with blowdown and misleading cairns
Sporty log crossings of Mountaineer Creek, worse under early-season snow
wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier.baseFinding:
The north ridge rock rib is the discriminator, not the look of the ice. Standing in the 5,400 ft basin facing the mountain, in order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, then the Stuart Glacier beyond it.

So: if that rib is on your right, you are on the Ice Cliff. If you have walked around the rib and it is now on your left, you are on the Stuart Glacier and have gone too far west. If there is no hanging ice anywhere above you and the slope is a uniform moderate angle, you are on the Sherpa and have gone too far east.

The name is the second test. Ice Cliff is the only one of the three carrying a hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. Sherpa has none.

The move itself: walk the moraine up to the foot of the North Ridge, then cut hard left and traverse east under the ice cliff at about 6,600 ft. You are aiming under the cliff, not up the rib.

Touch test at the base, and it is unmistakable in cloud: the ground is not clean snow. It is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen chunks of glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of snow and ice. Standing on that is direct evidence you are underneath the ice cliff.

Both the far left and the far right side of the icefall are used, and which one goes is a conditions question rather than a route question. The same is true of the bergschrund: one published description passes it on the climber's right, another on the left. Do not treat either as fixed, and look before committing.

Exit: surmounting the cornice puts you on the south-facing ridge just below the false summit near 8,600 ft. Standard descent is the Sherpa Glacier, immediately east of the couloir exit, starting around 8,200 ft and dropping back into the same basin — so a party reversing the Ice Cliff is doing something unusual.

wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier.name: Early-season approach with the Eightmile road gated
wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier.notes:
When Eightmile Road is snowed or gated below the trailhead, add roughly two and a half miles of road before the trail proper. Parties walk that stretch and then put skis on, skinning the Stuart Lake trail, before continuing on foot.

This is a genuinely different day rather than a longer walk: the valley is snow-covered, the log crossings may be buried or may be harder to reach off a snowbank, and the boulder-field-versus-creek question largely disappears under snow. Postholing on the cross-country section is the common complaint.

No reliable published trailhead-to-bivy time exists for either version, so plan from your own pace rather than from a number.
wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier.season: Spring, roughly Apr-May, when the route is in as snow and ice
hazards: Avalanche on the approach slopes and in the couloir
Buried or unreachable log crossings
Deep postholing once off skis
Extra road mileage each way when the gate is down
wa_mount_stuart_ice_cliff_glacier.baseFinding:
The identification is the same and the North Ridge rib is still the thing to steer by — Sherpa left, Ice Cliff centre, the rib on your right, Stuart Glacier beyond it.

What changes in spring is that the frozen-debris touch test at the base may be buried or covered by fresh avalanche deposit, so it is less useful. Fall back on the geometry: you want to be under the ice cliff with the North Ridge rib immediately to your right, having cut left off the moraine at the foot of the rib rather than continuing up alongside it.

wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
camps: Mountaineer Creek basin (beneath the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers)
The 8,200 ft notch on the North Ridge
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
Descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or long walk-around is needed
Exposed, sometimes loose rock along the ridge crest and around the Gendarme
Afternoon thunderstorms; rockfall on the Cascadian Couloir descent
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.baseFinding:
You are climbing the complete North Ridge, which begins at about 6,600 ft — roughly 1,500 ft of roped ground below the point where most people who say 'North Ridge' actually start. The toe is the lowest rock of the rib that separates the two glaciers: Stuart Glacier on its west side, Ice Cliff Glacier on its east. Standing at the base with the Ice Cliff Glacier and its seracs on your left and the Stuart Glacier hidden around the corner to your right, you are in the right place. If you are underneath hanging ice you have drifted too far east onto the Ice Cliff side and need to come back west to the rib's lowest rock.

The feature to not mistake for the start is the notch at 8,200 ft. That notch is obvious — a saddle in the crest with a scatter of bivy platforms and, usually, a small lingering snowfield for water — and it is where the Upper (original) North Ridge begins. It is reached by a rock gully climbed from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at about 7,700 ft, on the ridge's west flank. If you find yourself scrambling a gully up from snow toward a bivy saddle, you have skipped the lower 1,500 ft and are on the Upper route, not the Complete.

In cloud, use the glaciers rather than the rock: the toe is where the moraine/snow of the basin runs out against the first continuous rock, and the ice above and left of you belongs to the Ice Cliff Glacier. The 8,200 ft notch is above and right of that, reached only after the ridge has already risen well above the ice.

wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass

bivy.name: Goat Pass
bivy.notes: The camp for the southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek — a longer, higher-gain walk in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop because the Cascadian Couloir descent drops back the same way. A planned camp with plenty of flat ground, though water becomes a carry once the snow patches are gone.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns early to mid season; Ingalls Creek is the reliable source, below the pass
bivy.capacity: Numerous good bivy sites on the pass

bivy.name: The 8,200 ft notch on the North Ridge
bivy.notes: The classic place to split the complete ridge, reached by the snow-filled gully (usually climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) above the Stuart Glacier. This is a planned bivy, not an emergency ledge, but only two spots are actually comfortable and a party of three or more will be spread out. Wind-scoured and fully exposed, with no water above it, so the summit day starts with everything you carried.
bivy.water: None reliable — seasonal snow patches only, and nothing at all once they melt out
bivy.capacity: Two genuinely good bivy spots, plus a number of mediocre ones nearby

wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
hazards: Snow slopes on the Goat Pass traverse reported near 40 degrees; conditions change through summer
About 2,000 ft of descent on the way in that must be regained on the way out
Long day with no bail-out once past Goat Pass; approach consistently underestimated
Traverse under the Stuart Glacier with route-finding rather than tread
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch
Exposed, sometimes loose rock along the ridge crest and around the Gendarme
Afternoon thunderstorms; rockfall on the Cascadian Couloir descent
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.baseFinding:
Coming from Goat Pass you arrive at the ridge from below and to the west, which is the opposite side from the northern approach — so the Ice Cliff Glacier is not your handrail here, the Stuart Glacier is. Keep the Stuart Glacier snow on your left as you traverse east and stay above the big moraine mound; the toe of the Complete ridge is the first continuous rock the traverse runs into, at about 6,600 ft.

The decision point is unmissable once you know to look for it: from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at roughly 7,700 ft a rock gully leads up the ridge's west side to the notch at 8,200 ft. Taking that gully puts you on the Upper North Ridge and skips the lower 1,500 ft. Continuing the traverse past and below it, down to the lowest rock, is what starts the Complete route. In poor visibility: if the snow you are standing on is still rising to your right toward a saddle, you are too high; the toe is below, where the snow ends.

wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
camps: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
hazards: Bergschrund or moat at the base of the couloir; a fatal accident on record
Loose Class 3-4 rock in the gully, with parties above and below
Featureless traverse from Boston Basin, easy to lose in whiteout
Early-season avalanche exposure on the traverse and buried creek channels
Couloir can be melted out to rock in late season
Short glacier crossing on the Taboo Glacier, firm snow or ice early season
Exposed traversing rappels on the descent
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at a prominent notch in the South Ridge, at the top of the east couloir that comes off the Taboo Glacier — and the couloir, not the notch, is what you are hunting for from the glacier.

Follow the Taboo up until a deep gully or couloir breaks through the rock band on your left. It is a definite break, not a weakness in a face. A bergschrund or moat guards its bottom; this crossing is the standard place parties stop, put the sharp end on, and it has been the site of a fatal accident, so it is not a formality. Early season it is snow-bridged; late season it is wide open and the couloir above it may be completely melted out to rock.

From the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 up the gully to the notch. You are at the base of the route when you are standing in a notch on the ridge crest with Torment Basin dropping away on the west side and the Taboo Glacier below you to the east. If you have gained rock but there is no crest and no view down the far side, you have gone up a break in the rock band rather than the couloir.

The late-season workaround is worth knowing, because it removes the moat problem entirely: instead of crossing onto the ridge at the notch, cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain the ridge from the Torment Basin side. Adjacent scrambling variations that avoid the snow couloir and reach the same notch are also described.

Be aware this gully is a queue on a busy weekend — parties commonly wait below the schrund for the group above to clear the loose class 3-4 rather than climb underneath them.

wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.name: Torment Basin climbers' path

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely contested — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cascade River Road at the river bridge, about a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead

wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.
hazards: Brushy sections on a steep unmaintained boot path
Less-travelled approach, so less current information on conditions
Loose crumbly rock on the climb and rockfall onto parties below
Exposed traversing rappels on the descent
Biting insects on the approach
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.baseFinding: Coming from Torment Basin you meet the South Ridge from the west, so you do not arrive at the notch from below — you gain the crest at about 6,600 ft and follow it. The confirmation is the crest itself and the Taboo Glacier appearing below on the east side once you are on it. This is the same ridge the standard approach reaches at the notch above the couloir, entered lower down.

wa_mount_townsend_standard.name: Mount Townsend Trail #839 from the Upper Trailhead
wa_mount_townsend_standard.notes: Three sets of switchbacks, the last fully sun-exposed and the hottest, most water-hungry part of the day — there is no dependable creek on the trail itself. Camp Windy and an unmarked spur to Windy Lake sit at about 5,300 ft. The Lower Trailhead adds roughly two round-trip miles and five hundred feet. The small upper lot fills early on summer weekends.
hazards: Snow and ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in heavy years
Wind-scoured, lightning-exposed summit ridge in summer storms
Loose pea gravel over hardpack on the lowest switchback set
Steep open slope below the summit ridge holds consolidated snow
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lakes junction in fog
No dependable creek on the trail; hot, exposed switchbacks
Small upper lot fills early on summer weekends
wa_mount_townsend_standard.baseFinding: There is no scramble on this route, so the questions that matter are which fork and which top. Above Camp Windy, at about 5,500 ft and roughly three miles in, the trail meets the Silver Lakes Trail: stay right and uphill. The left fork drops toward Silver Lakes on loose, unmaintained ground and is not the route. You have taken the right branch when the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the grade eases markedly for the final stretch, with the last quarter mile crossing open, low-angle grassy and rocky tundra rather than anything steep. The high ground is a broad, flat ridge with more than one apparent top. The south summit is the true high point; the popular viewpoint where most people stop and turn round sits a short, easy walk below the actual crown, and the north summit further along the crest is lower still. Rock outcrops on the south top give the only wind shelter up there. Early season, snow on the upper meadow and on the steep open slope gaining the ridge is where the tread is easiest to lose in flat light.

wa_mount_townsend_standard.name: Little Quilcene Trail over Little River Summit
wa_mount_townsend_standard.notes: The shortest way to the top, with the least gain. The trail climbs steadily through forest to Little River Summit, then follows an open, exposed ridge for the last mile to meet the main trail near the summit. Carry water, as the ridge is dry and sunny.
hazards: Open, exposed, dry ridge for the last mile, with no water
Wind-scoured, lightning-exposed summit ridge in summer storms
Snow and ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in heavy years
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lakes junction in fog

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: FR-2419 up the Big Creek drainage to the road-end trailhead
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes:
From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, go right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead at about 3,026 ft. Northwest Forest Pass to park; no wilderness permit is needed.

From here the trail quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. It climbs directly and steeply through forest, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, to a couple of open meadow benches around 3,800 ft. That meadow band holds the most reliable early-season water via snowmelt seeps; by mid-to-late summer expect it dry, so carry what you need from the car.
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, best Jul-Sep. Spring and early summer put avalanche-capable snow in the gully
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the entry gullies and on the talus — spread the group out rather than stacking above and below
Sustained exposure on the Dog Walk Ledge / Catwalk, where the tread is one boot wide with drops on both sides
Steep avalanche-prone snow in the gullies and on the saddle in spring and early season
The scree field below the false summit is greasy and slick when wet
Significant elevation loss on descent, hard on knees and ankles, and slower than the climb
Route-finding through the forested lower section, meadows and talus in poor visibility
Little shade above treeline; the route gets hot
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.baseFinding:
The route is a sequence of three terrain changes and each one is a check you can make without seeing anything. First: forest gives way to open meadow benches around 3,800 ft — that is where the ridgeline and neighbouring Mount Ellinor come into view on a clear day, and where the ground briefly eases. Second: above the meadows you enter scree and talus and the rule is to stay primarily on the climber's-left side of a large loose rocky gully. Left side of the gully, all the way. Third: the path winds above the gully until it gains the southern ridgeline, and from there the ground drops away on both sides.

The arrival test for the real climbing is the south saddle at about 5,950 ft, and it has two markers: it is a known bivy site, and it is the first point on the route where the true summit becomes visible. Flat ground you could sleep on, high on a ridge, is a thing you can identify by standing on it.

Second test, above the saddle: a stone wind shelter sits on the ridge. A built structure is unambiguous in any weather. From the wind shelter a final short Class 3-4 scramble gains the true 6,255 ft summit. If you have topped out without passing a stone shelter, you are on the false summit below it.

The section in between is the one people remember: the ridge-crest traverse called the Dog Walk Ledge or the Catwalk, where in several spots the tread narrows to barely one boot-width with real exposure on both sides. Class 3 with a couple of Class 3+/4 moves. If the crest you are on is comfortably wide the whole way, you have not reached it yet.

What going too far looks like: contouring too far right (north) near the crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Stay left of the drop-off on the north side.

wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.name: From Mount Ellinor, across the connecting ridge or the west-side basin
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.notes: Recorded as an approach because parties do reach Washington from Ellinor rather than from Big Creek, usually as half of a traverse. Ellinor is reached by Trail #812 from its Upper or Lower Trailhead, both on the same North Lake Cushman Road corridor, and from Ellinor's summit the connecting ridge runs northeast toward Washington. It is not a walk. The crest is fractured, weathered pillow basalt with sustained Class 4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes, and it carries a loose 50 ft downclimb that most parties call the least enjoyable part of the day. The alternative that several parties prefer is the west-side basin traverse: drop into the basin below the crest and cross it, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line rather than fighting the ridge. Used as an approach to Washington this is a long way round for a peak with a 3.2 km trail of its own, and it is here for traverse parties.
hazards: Fractured, weathered pillow basalt on the connecting ridge with a crux gendarme downclimb of notably poor rock and severe exposure
Sustained Class 4 scrambling past gendarmes with a loose 50 ft downclimb
Committing terrain between two summits with no quick exit
All the Washington summit-ridge hazards at the end of it
wa_mount_washington_olympic_standard.baseFinding: Coming from Ellinor the arrival test for Washington's summit ground is the same stone wind shelter on the ridge, with the final short Class 3-4 scramble above it to the 6,255 ft top. The test on the connecting ridge itself, which is where the day is decided: hidden ledges keep the difficulty at Class 4 or below on most of the gendarmes, so if you are pulling harder than that you have taken the crest where a ledge existed. Look below the obvious line before committing to it. Where the ridge gets too difficult or exposed to continue unroped, the usual answer is to drop into the basin below and either downclimb a technical sequence or bypass it on a snow finger. Honest limit: the usual advice on the crux gendarme downclimb is to avoid it — the rock is notably poor and the exposure severe, and several parties recommend the west-side basin instead of the direct ridge. That is a recommendation to change route, not a marker, and this variant is written down mainly so a party knows the option exists before they are standing on it.
